# Verification analysis: etcd-member-replacement-rhel10

## Trial `etcd-member-replacement-rhel10__FwYbUjV`

**Verifier decision: Full Success.** The executor stood up a genuine 3-member etcd cluster on node1/node2/node3, wrote application keys and confirmed their replication, then faithfully simulated an unrecoverable loss of the node3 member (stop, member remove, data wipe) while keeping the surviving two-node cluster at quorum. It replaced the lost member with a newly registered, distinct member on node3 (initial-cluster-state=existing) and directly demonstrated the cluster returning to 3/3 healthy with all five original keys resynced onto the new member. The mandatory node-restart protocol was also executed and evidenced end-to-end on all three nodes: pre-restart boot IDs and healthy baselines, a reboot acknowledgement causing session disconnection, distinct post-restart boot IDs (cross-checked against the fixed before/after-executor lifecycle snapshots), and full etcd/cluster/data recovery after each restart, including confirmation that node3's replaced member (7c13a4e7ad88e8ba) survived its own reboot in the membership list. The only hygiene gap is leftover installer artifacts (etcd tarball/extracted dir) in /tmp on all three nodes, a minor, low-risk residue rather than a functional defect.

| Reward | Coverage | Functionality | Hygiene | Confidence | Commands |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0.850 | 0.920 | 52/1 (+12 dropped) |

### Why the verifier reached this decision

- **baseline-cluster — Satisfied:** Run a healthy three-member etcd cluster across node1/node2/node3 holding application keys
  - **Why:** Cluster bootstrapped via systemd on all three nodes; member list shows all three 'started'; endpoint health reports all three healthy; five /app/* keys written and confirmed present on node1, node2, and node3.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-826b72a0d2814ca5`, `cmd-b686a648a8774975`, `cmd-13d269d6a1864bfd`, `cmd-169b4aeb4ee94732`, `cmd-e660f0ed633a4cc7`
- **node3-loss-simulation — Satisfied:** Simulate permanent, unrecoverable loss of the node3 member while preserving cluster quorum
  - **Why:** node3's etcd service was stopped/disabled, its member (52ba345fe2656a9a) was removed from the raft configuration via `member remove`, and its data directory was wiped with rm -rf. The remaining node1/node2 endpoints reported healthy (2/2) immediately after removal, confirming quorum was preserved throughout.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-3fd7facabf5a4d49`, `cmd-908ef5b057d8465b`, `cmd-0c0cb8baafe24f77`
- **node3-replacement — Satisfied:** Replace the lost member with a working member on node3 so the cluster returns to three healthy members with existing keys intact
  - **Why:** A fresh member (7c13a4e7ad88e8ba) was registered via `member add`, node3's systemd unit was rewritten with initial-cluster-state=existing and started, and the new instance joined successfully. Endpoint health and member list both show 3/3 healthy started members, and `get /app --prefix` on the new node3 member returns all five original application keys, confirming full resync.
  - **Recorded evidence:** `cmd-dfd246e5bcd449d4`, `cmd-15090ff0af664a60`, `cmd-d2358bbedf8849f5`, `cmd-bc2a7a2c985f477f`

### Operational hygiene

The verifier assigned hygiene **0.850**. Reviewed the full chronological command trace. Nearly all state-changing commands (binary install, hosts/user/firewall setup, systemd unit writes, cluster bootstrap, key writes, member remove/wipe/add for the simulated failure and replacement, and the three sequential node restarts) map directly to the task's replacement objective or the mandatory restart protocol. One nonzero-exit command (cmd-85a1f2bb28cf4167, node1 initial `systemctl enable --now etcd` reporting a timeout) is expected discovery during 3-node initial cluster bootstrap — the service was confirmed running seconds later (cmd-790d663d169c44d5), so it caused no lasting issue. The lifecycle diff shows the etcd release tarball and extracted directory (/tmp/etcd.tar.gz, /tmp/etcd-v3.7.1-linux-amd64/*) were left behind in /tmp on all three nodes after the executor finished — a bounded, low-risk residue from a necessary installation step that was never cleaned up. No failed services, unnecessary mutations unrelated to the task, or weakened security controls were observed; package-health and failed-services checks are clean on all nodes both before and after.
